newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish Solidarity sees growth as top economic goal.
newsitem.headline: Polish Solidarity sees growth as top economic goal.

text.p: Faster growth and privatisation will top the economic agenda of Poland's Solidarity-led rightist alliance when it announces its election programme next month, the Solidarity union's spokesman said on Monday.
"Only faster growth will allow us to achieve such goals as social security reform, the reduction of unemployment, growth of real incomes and limiting poverty," Piotr Zak told Reuters.
The Polish economy grew by about six percent last year after seven percent growth in 1995 and is forecast to expand by a further 5.5 percent this year.

But Zak, whose union leads Solidarity Election Action (AWS), grouping more than 30 rightist parties set to challenge the ruling left in this year's parliamentary polls, said that without sweeping reforms Poland's growth would lose momentum.

Zak said AWS, which plans to translate its election programme into a set of draft laws shortly before the polls due in September or October, wanted to spur growth with lower taxes, investment incentives and overhauled privatisation.
Solidarity charges that privatisation now benefits only political elites and their supporters, while privatisation revenues are treated as a huge slush fund for vote-winning programmes.

He said AWS wanted sales of such major firms as banks, copper firm KGHM Polska Miedz and telecoms monopoly TPSA to combine offers to strategic investors with free shares for employees, the public and stakes set aside for pension funds.
"We want to combine offers for strategic investors with mass privatisation," he said.
Asked whether AWS would try to put on hold schemes like the KGHM offer which were already underway, Zak said:
"We will use all legal means to prevent public wealth being taken over by the present political establishment."
Zak said in the interview that AWS had yet to decide whether there were industries or firms that should stay off-limits for privatisation or foreign investment.
But he said AWS was generally open to and saw room for foreign investment even in such strategic areas as arms.
"There is no other chance for our defence sector than cooperation with firms from our future NATO partners," he said.
He also said AWS saw no alternative to European Union membership but believed some hard bargaining was necessary to win entry on the best possible terms.

"Any ideas for development outside of the EU are a recipe for Poland staying in Russia's economic and political sphere of influence...but we should not only adjust to the EU, we should also voice demands for what we want from the union," he said.
Zak said AWS was keen to disprove allegations by the ruling ex-communists and others that once in power it would print money to spend on education, health and fighting unemployment.

"The reds (ex-communists) are now using the method that democratic forces deployed against them four years ago, and present themselves as the only sensible force surrounded by a bunch of economic charlatans," he said.
The ruling left claims credit for keeping budget deficits below three percent of gross domestic product for the last four years and aims at a 2.8 percent shortfall this year.
Zak said AWS would be just as prudent and would seek to improve efficiency by moving funds to local governments from the central budget and other measures.
"Budget discipline is a key issue...and AWS coming to power will not mean printing money," he said.
"Incurring debts, which will be paid by future generations if made irresponsibly, is not only economically unsound but is also unethical," he said.
